awd_titl_txt: Travel: NSF Student Travel Grant for the 2025 Consortium for the Science of Sociotechnical Systems Summer Research Institute (CSST 2025)
awd_abstract_narration:
This award will support 11 PhD students attending the Consortium for the Science of Sociotechnical Systems (CSST) Summer Research Institute.  Many of humanity's most pressing problems require research teams that can bring together both social and technical expertise.  For instance, improving cybersecurity and privacy requires deep technical knowledge of encryption and trust models, as well as philosophical and anthropological understandings of values like safety and autonomy.  The researchers, data scientists, and designers who will solve these "socio-technical" problems need need training in interdisciplinary thinking and collaboration. However, researchers who span boundaries too often are trained at the margins of their fields and lack models of success, mentorship, or support in their home institutions and fields. The CSST Summer Research Institute provides this support by bringing together senior Ph.D. students, post-docs, industry researchers, and early career faculty with experienced boundary-spanning researchers, providing a critical intellectual and professional support system that enables boundary-spanning researchers to succeed in both their careers and the social problems they tackle.

The central function of the institute is to sustain and develop a densely connected research community of scholars. An initial cohort of approximately 10 mentors are recruited each fall, with additional mentors recruited as needed to support the particular needs of mentees in the spring. The call for participants is released in early spring each year. Approximately 30 participants (senior Ph.D. students, post-docs, industry researchers, and early career faculty) are chosen by a review committee comprised of mentors, organizers, and other senior reviewers as necessary to conduct a well-informed review of the submissions; these reviewers will make their decisions based on materials submitted by applicants in response to the Call for Participation. Disciplinary, methodological, institutional, and topical breath will all be considered in final acceptance decisions. Participants will be invited to join informal social activities outside of the institute's formal sessions and participate in a Slack workspace intended to support cohort and community beyond the conclusion of the in-person event.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
The Consortium for the Science of Sociotechnical Systems (CSST) Summer Research Institute is an intensive mentoring and career development program for early-career researchers who study how technology and society shape one another. These researchers work across computer science, information science, sociology, communication, health, education, and related fields. Because their work spans disciplines, they often lack mentors, role models, and supportive communities in their home departments. This award supported travel, lodging, and meals for doctoral students to attend the 2025 Institute, held May 28 to June 1, 2025, at the Minnowbrook Conference Center in Blue Mountain Lake, New York.

The Institute brought together 21 early-career researchers and 7 senior mentors, along with 3 organizers. The early-career participants came from 18 universities in the United States and Canada. They included 16 doctoral students (11 of whom were funded by this award), 3 postdoctoral researchers, and 2 junior faculty members, and several were in the middle of moving into postdoctoral or faculty positions. Their research addressed questions such as how digital platforms shape gig and platform work, how technology can support mental health and emergency medical care, how content moderation affects communities outside the West, and how government data systems affect cities and residents.

The program combined sustained mentoring with interactive workshops. Each mentor worked with a small group of three participants, grouped by career stage and research interests, through small-group sessions, one-on-one conversations, and shared meals. Six workshop sessions covered introducing one's research to others, navigating interdisciplinary publishing, collaboration and identity, research funding and paths to impact beyond academia, the career journeys of senior researchers, and crafting a scholarly identity and research "pitch" for different audiences. The funding session brought in perspectives on federal agencies, including an NSF program officer, as well as industry and private foundations. A final session focused on how participants could sustain the community after the Institute. The remote setting was intentional. With few distractions, participants had extended time for the kind of candid conversation that is hard to find at large conferences.

Intellectual Merit: The Institute advanced sociotechnical research by creating a space where researchers from different disciplines could examine how their work fits together and what defines a sociotechnical research agenda. The organizers developed a set of openly available resources that participants used during the Institute and continue to use afterward (https://csst2025.github.io). These include a funding landscape guide covering federal, foundation, industry, and international sources, a taxonomy of research impact pathways with an interactive impact-planning tool, a proposal development worksheet, and toolkits for translating research across disciplines and presenting it to different audiences. In the exit survey, participants repeatedly named these resources as useful for future grant writing and job applications. Several said they had not encountered such structured guidance before.

Broader Impacts: The Institute is part of a long-running effort to train researchers who can work across the boundary between social and technical fields, a need that grows as technologies like AI reshape work, health, education, and public life. The 2025 cohort was diverse in discipline, institution, and career stage, and most early-career participants were women. Twelve of the 21 early-career participants and 6 of the 7 mentors completed an exit survey. Every respondent rated their sense of connection to the CSST community at 5 or higher on a 7-point scale, with an average of 6.2. Participants most valued the small-group and one-on-one mentoring, which gave them guidance outside the power dynamics of their home institutions. They also valued the scholarly identity session, which many said sharpened how they explain their research to hiring committees and other audiences. And they valued hearing senior researchers describe their own non-linear career paths. One participant wrote that this was the first time in their doctoral program they felt part of an academic community. Another said the impact session changed their belief that only high-profile scholars can make a difference.

The Institute's effects are designed to extend beyond the event itself. Mentors reported that they plan to continue mentoring their groups. Participants proposed, and many volunteered to help build, continuing activities including an online alumni community, dissertation-writing and job-market support groups, and a research-focused CSST gathering where participants can get feedback on work in progress. Participant feedback on scheduling, mentor rotation, and more time to discuss research in depth will inform the design of future Institutes. In these ways, the 2025 Institute strengthened a sustained network that supports the next generation of sociotechnical researchers.
